title: Start with Why
author: Simon Sinek
theme: Leaders and organisations that inspire lasting loyalty communicate their purpose first, and only then explain how they work and what they offer.
summary: Simon Sinek asks why a small number of leaders and companies manage to inspire people again and again, while most others, with similar resources and talent, do not. His answer is a simple model he calls the Golden Circle: three rings with Why at the centre, How around it, and What on the outside.

Every organisation knows what it does, and many know how they do it. Few can state why they exist beyond making money. Most communicate from the outside in, leading with features and price. Inspiring organisations reverse the order. They begin with a belief or cause, then describe the way they act on it, and only then present the product as proof.

Sinek argues that this pattern follows the structure of the human brain. The newer, rational part handles facts and language, while older parts drive feelings, trust and decisions but have no capacity for words. Messages that start with purpose speak to the part of us that decides, which is why people often say a choice simply feels right.

He contrasts inspiration with manipulation. Discounts, promotions, fear, novelty and peer pressure can win a sale, but they are costly, short-lived and build no loyalty. People who share your belief, by contrast, stay with you and recommend you.

The model also explains how ideas spread. Sinek draws on the diffusion of innovations curve, noting that the mass market only follows once enough innovators and early adopters, who buy for what they believe, have committed first.

To keep the circle intact, leaders need clarity of purpose, discipline in how values are applied, and consistency in everything the organisation says and does. Trouble often starts when a founder leaves and success turns the focus to results alone, so the purpose fades.
The lasting lesson is that people do not buy what you do; they commit to the belief behind it.
takeaway: Know and state your purpose clearly, then make every decision and product a consistent expression of it.

questions.q: What sits at the centre of Sinek's Golden Circle?
questions.why: Purpose, the Why, is the core from which How and What should follow.

questions.q: In what order do inspiring organisations communicate, according to Sinek?
questions.why: They work from the inside out, leading with their belief and using the product as proof of it.

questions.q: How does Sinek say most organisations communicate?
options: Starting with what they sell and its features
questions.why: Most lead from the outside in, talking about products, features and price.

questions.q: Why does starting with purpose influence decisions so strongly, in Sinek's account?
options: It is backed by detailed statistics
It appeals to the brain areas that govern feeling and decision-making
It reduces the price customers pay
It is easier to put in advertising
questions.why: He links Why to the older parts of the brain that drive trust and decisions but do not process language.

questions.q: Which of these does Sinek treat as a form of manipulation rather than inspiration?
options: Hiring people who share the cause
questions.why: Discounts and promotions can drive a sale but create no lasting loyalty.

questions.q: What is Sinek's main criticism of manipulative tactics?
options: They work in the short term but are costly and build no loyalty
They only work for small firms
questions.why: Manipulations can be effective transactionally, but they must be repeated and earn no commitment.

questions.q: According to the diffusion of innovations idea Sinek uses, who must be won over before the mass market follows?
questions.why: The mainstream only joins once enough early buyers, who act on belief, have committed.

questions.q: Which trio does Sinek say keeps an organisation's Golden Circle in balance?
options: Clarity of Why, discipline of How, consistency of What
Low cost, high speed, wide reach
questions.why: Purpose must be clear, values applied with discipline, and actions consistent with both.

questions.q: According to Sinek, what often happens when a founder leaves a successful company?
options: Its sense of Why can fade as attention shifts to results alone
It must change its products immediately
questions.why: Without the person who embodied the cause, success can turn the focus to what and how, and the purpose blurs.

questions.q: What is the book's central message about why people commit to a company or leader?
options: They commit to the belief behind what is offered
questions.why: Sinek's core claim is that people buy into why you do something, not just what you do.
